subject: Measurement invariance: impact of releasing the equality constraints

messages.author: c8172cf47ead82fa
messages.subject: Measurement invariance: impact of releasing the equality constraints
parts:
In my multiple group model (2 groups) I have weak measurement invariance. So I estimated the impact of releasing the quality constraints:

lhs op rhs group free label plabel    est    epc    epv
76  BP ~1         2   67        .p76.  0.160 -0.010  0.150
77  CO ~1         2   68        .p77. -0.067  0.007 -0.060
78 FMO ~1         2   69        .p78.  0.098 -0.033  0.064

How should I interpret the epc values? I have read the Oberski (2014) paper but there seems no rule of thumb available.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance: impact of releasing the equality constraints
parts: How should I interpret the epc values? I have read the Oberski (2014) paper but there seems no rule of thumb available.

There isn't a rule of thumb; they should be interpreted relative to the scale of the variables.  Hopefully standardized EPCs will be added to this output soon, and the guideline for SEPCs is that changes < 0.1 are not large, but that is just a rule of thumb.  

Since these are just means, it is pretty easy to standardize them yourself.  Just divide each EPC by the total variance of that variable, which you can find on the diagonal of lavInspect(fit, "cov.all")

Note, however, that these are the EPCs assuming that ALL constraints listed in the univariate tests are released.  If you want to know the EPC(-interest) associated with releasing one/each particular constraint, you should look at the EPCs from individual runs of lavTestScore() where only that one constraint is released.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Measurement invariance: impact of releasing the equality constraints
parts: Is there a reference I can look up for the rul of thumb on standardized EPCs?

Kaplan (1989) recommended SEPC < .10

https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327906mbr2403_2

Saris et al. (2009) recommended SEPC < .20

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705510903203433

See also Whitaker's (2012) simulation study

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/00220973.2010.531299
